title: Idris and the Cosmic Cat
markdown:
The Starlight Spire Observatory clung to the mountaintop like a silver cap. Inside, beneath a dome that swivelled like a giant half-waking, Idris wrestled not with a faraway star but with a grant proposal that seemed determined to steal the sparkle from his life. Overseeing the desk, with regal disinterest, was Fen, the observatory cat. Fen was the boss. His stare spoke volumes about Idris’s coffee habits and issued a silent demand for more treats.

“It’s just the words,” Idris sighed, ruffling already messy hair. “‘Potential paradigm shift’? Sounds like I’m peddling a used spaceship.” A tightness squeezed his chest, the familiar flutter that arrived whenever he tried to explain big ideas. They would think he was reaching too far, or worse, making it up. Fen, perched on a tower of journals, let out a low purr remarkably like a weary sigh. Daily routine: Idris wrestling with words and money; Fen silently judging from on high.

Then, one Tuesday, the hum of machines and the rustle of papers stopped. The console flickered with a pattern they had never seen. A strange signal pulsed on the main screen. Idris’s eyes widened. A discovery. His heart performed a giddy jig, then a tremor of doubt. This could put him on the map. Headlines. No more second-guessing a career. Fen, usually as calm as a moonbeam, chirped and hopped onto the desk. He sniffed the console with the keen interest he reserved for tuna, tail twitching.

“What do you think, Fen?” Idris whispered.

Fen extended a paw, tapped the screen, and gave Idris a long deliberate look: hold your horses. Could be a glitch. Or a rogue pigeon. Later that day the director announced, tie collection as loud as his declarations, that the observatory’s funding depended on a significant published discovery within the month. A clock ticked louder than any exploding star. Cold dread settled in Idris’s stomach. The stakes, recently distant, now sat on the desk beside Fen.

Idris dedicated days to the signal, nights to dreaming in code, fingers dancing across the keyboard. The more he looked, the stranger it became: layered, hidden, frustratingly occulted in noise. Then Dr. Aris Thorne arrived from the rival institution on the mountain, smile sharp as a new lens, faintly smelling of expensive cologne. Thorne’s ego was rumoured to be visible from space. He appeared whenever good news was brewing or glory was within reach, a weather system of ambition.

“Idris, my boy,” Thorne boomed, startling Fen from a nap. “Heard you’re poking around something interesting. Mind if I have a look? For science, of course.”

Idris felt the familiar prickle. Thorne’s “for science” often meant Thorne collecting the praise, and perhaps a prime parking spot.

Fen flattened his ears and growled, a sound usually reserved for a plump mouse. This was worse. He positioned himself between Thorne and the console, tail a furry pendulum of defiance. Thorne chuckled, unbothered.

Idris stood at a crossroads he knew too well. He could rush the analysis, claim a small discovery to satisfy funders and impress Thorne, feed the old fear of vanishing into obscurity. He looked at Fen, calmly blocking the advance, then at the baffling data. What if he hurried and ruined his name? Thorne would never let him forget. Fen’s earlier nudge had been a reminder to be careful. He had to be sure.

Thorne smirked, sensing hesitation.

“No, Dr. Thorne,” Idris said, voice surprisingly steady. “The data isn’t complete. It needs more careful study. We’re not ready for outside opinions.”

The smirk vanished. Thorne huffed, grumbled about impatient youngsters, and retreated.

Days blurred. The signal clarified into astonishingly complex patterns: not merely a new object, but something fundamentally different. Idris and Fen worked without stopping. Fen nudged misplaced disks back into place and batted pens that threatened Idris’s focus. His purrs were a low constant of support. One evening, deadline looming, Idris found a hidden layer, a marker pointing to an extraordinary cosmic event discussed only in hushed academic tones. The analysis was massive. It would strain the main computer. Risky. Possibly brilliant.

Thorne reappeared with a team, clipboards like weapons, unwarranted confidence. “We’re here to help. My team has a better calculation method. We can finish by morning and ensure proper credit, naturally.”

The knot of anxiety tightened. Thorne wanted the glory. Then Fen, in a leap that defied gravity and HR policy, landed squarely on Thorne’s head. Perfectly styled hair went askew. The clipboard flew. Chaos: indignant yelps, scattered papers. Fen, immensely satisfied, batted at Thorne’s ankles, a four-legged roadblock.

Amid the pandemonium, as assistants scrambled for notes, Idris understood. He could not let Thorne claim this. The discovery belonged to the work. He turned to Clara, his eager research assistant, who had been watching with wide eyes.

“Clara, I need your help with the computation. We’ll share the processing. It might overload the system, but we have to try. We need the real data out there.”

He was willing to risk the observatory’s function not for fame but for the truth. Screens bloomed with numbers and graphs. Machinery hummed, thrilling and terrifying. Ozone mixed with nervous sweat and the warm scent of Fen’s fur. The cat, mission accomplished, settled on Idris’s lap, purring. Thorne’s assistants typed a distant, frantic rhythm against their own steadier beat.

By sunrise the signal was decoded. Not merely a new body: proof of a theorized cosmic event, a rare alignment confirming fundamental physics, the sort of finding that rewrites textbooks. Idris, Clara, and a slightly rumpled Thorne—thoroughly outsmarted by a feline—stood before a panel of distinguished scientists. Idris, Clara beside him, presented the findings. He spoke of shared effort and careful checking. He even mentioned Fen’s management skills. He did not need to be the only hero. Fen quietly enjoyed a saucer of cream from a grateful Clara, accepting it with the dignity of a cat who had navigated a corporate takeover.

Later, Starlight Spire buzzed with genuine excitement. Idris worked a new grant proposal, writing clearer, hand steady. He looked up at the stars without the old sting of doubt. Fen, curled on his usual perch, sighed contentedly. The tremor of ambition in his human had become a hum of purpose. The dome turned, slow and sure, toward whatever signal came next.
characters: Idris (a graduate astronomer), Fen (the observatory cat)
